items: Open the **Thermodynamics Lab** menu: **Part 1 · Simulation 1: Heat transfer and calorimetry**. Click **Guided** (top right).
Metal: **Iron**. Sample mass: **50 g** (◀ ▶ buttons, 5 g per click). Water: leave the vertical slider at **60 g** (water starts at **20 °C**).

Burner fire slider: **all the way right** (3 flames) = metal at **100 °C**. It goes back to the lowest setting (40 °C) every time the metal changes, so set it again. Check the formula line reads **−50 × 0.45 × ( □ − 100) = 60 × 4.2 × ( □ − 20)**.

items.prompt: Iron starts at 100 °C and the water at 20 °C. Will the final temperature be closer to 20 °C or to 100 °C? Why?
items.answer: Closer to 20 °C (the sim gives 26.6 °C). Water has a much larger specific heat (4.2 vs. 0.45 J/g·°C) and more mass, so it takes far more energy to warm the water. Accept any answer with a reason; the reason is what earns the point.

items: Energy cannot be {{destroyed}} or {{created}}. Energy is {{transferred}}.
Specific heat in the sim (J/g·°C): iron {{0.45}}, aluminum {{0.897}}, lithium {{3.58}}, water {{4.2}}.
Heat is transferred from the metal, the {{system}}, to the cold water, the {{surroundings}}.
Energy is conserved: heat goes from {{hot}} to {{cold}}. The metal {{loses}} heat and the water {{gains}} it until both reach T_f.
−q_system = q_surrounding
−mₛ × Cₛ × (T_f − T_i,s) = m_w × C_w × (T_f − T_i,w)

items.prompt: **Before you drag the tweezers,** calculate T_f for the iron run. Solving the equation above for T_f gives T_f = (mₛCₛT_i,s + m_wC_wT_i,w) ÷ (mₛCₛ + m_wC_w).

blocks.subtitle: Drag the tweezers onto the sample, then drop it into the calorimeter. The run starts by itself. Tap Next for the next metal (and reset the burner!).
blocks.note: T_f appears in the boxes of the formula line. Read q from the **right-hand box** of the bottom line (… J = ____ J). Fill the last row in Free Explore with your own settings.

items.prompt: Use q = m × c × ΔT and your T_f to calculate the heat gained by the water in the iron run. Then give q for the iron.
items.answer: q_water = 60 g × 4.2 J/g·°C × (26.6 − 20) °C = **1663 J ≈ 1.66 kJ**. q_iron = **−1663 J** (same size, opposite sign). Accept 1650–1665 J: the sim shows 1652 J because it uses the unrounded T_f (26.56 °C).

blocks.answer: Iron curve falls from 100 °C; water curve rises from 20 °C. Both change fast at first, then level off together at T_f = 26.6 °C.
blocks.subtitle: Sketch the temperature vs. time graph for the iron run. Label both curves and T_f.

items.prompt: Rank the three metals by T_f. Explain the ranking using specific heat. (Claim + evidence)
items.answer: Lithium (53.2 °C) > aluminum (32.1 °C) > iron (26.6 °C). Same mass and starting temperature, but lithium has the largest specific heat (3.58 vs. 0.897 vs. 0.45 J/g·°C), so it holds and gives up the most heat (8373 J vs. 3046 J vs. 1652 J) and warms the water most.

items.prompt: In the iron run, the iron cooled by 73.4 °C but the water warmed by only 6.6 °C. The heat was the same size. Why are the temperature changes so different?
items.answer: m × c is much larger for the water: 60 × 4.2 = 252 J/°C vs. 50 × 0.45 = 22.5 J/°C for iron. The same amount of heat changes the water's temperature about 11 times less. Accept: water has a higher specific heat and more mass.

items.prompt: Is the heat flow exothermic or endothermic for the iron (the system)? For the water? Use the sign of q.
items.answer: Exothermic for the iron: it loses heat, q_iron is negative (−1652 J). Endothermic for the water: it gains heat, q_water is positive (+1652 J). Heat stops flowing at thermal equilibrium (both at 26.6 °C).

blocks.text: Switch to **Free Explore**. Set the burner to the **lowest** setting (1 flame = 40 °C), or try 100 g of iron or 120 g of water. Predict T_f, run it, and fill in the last table row.

items: Open the menu: **Part 2 · Simulation 2: Energy diagrams, phases, and reaction enthalpy**. Click **Guided**. Choose a Substance: **Water**.
Every number in this part is for **1 g** of substance. The sim never shows the mass, but it is always 1 g.

Move the **heat slider** under the burner slowly right. Watch the thermometer, the speech bubble and the **Equations** box. **Stop** when the water boils at 100 °C and do the Calculate box before you slide further.

items.prompt: You keep adding heat to ice that is melting at 0 °C. What happens to the temperature while it melts? Why?
items.answer: It stays at 0 °C until all the ice has melted. The energy goes into breaking intermolecular forces, not into raising the temperature.

items: Enthalpy change under constant pressure is ΔH = Cₚ × (T₂ − T₁), where T₁ is the {{initial}} temperature and T₂ is the {{current}} temperature.
Cₚ depends on both the {{substance}} and its {{physical state}}. Solid water: Cₚ ≈ {{2.1}} J/g·°C. Liquid water: Cₚ = {{4.2}} J/g·°C.
ΔH_f, the enthalpy of {{fusion}}, accounts for the energy needed to {{melt}} the substance. For water, ΔH_f = {{333}} J.
During a change of phase, temperature stays {{constant}}, so ΔH = Cₚ × (T₂ − T₁) is {{zero}}. All the energy goes into breaking {{intermolecular forces}}.
ΔH_v, the enthalpy of {{vaporization}}, is {{2230}} J for water. Once fully vaporized, Cₚ becomes {{1.9}} J/g·°C.
ΔH = Cₚ × (T₂ − T₁)    (for 1 g; for m grams: q = m × Cₚ × ΔT)
ΔH_total = ΔH_f + ΔH_v + ΔH (one ΔH for each heating leg)

items.prompt: Use the sim's values in your notes to calculate the total heat needed to take 1 g of water from −10 °C to 120 °C. Show all five legs. Then slide to 120 °C and check your total against the last line of the Equations box.

blocks.subtitle: Choose Ethanol, then Acetone, and slide through each curve. Read melting and boiling points from the thermometer on the flat parts.
blocks.note: Read liquid Cₚ once the substance has melted (the speech bubble and the Equations box both show it then).

blocks.answer: Rising line (solid), flat at 0 °C (melting), rising line (liquid), flat at 100 °C (boiling), rising line (vapor). Accept any sketch with three rising legs, two flat legs, and correct labels.
blocks.subtitle: Sketch the heating curve for water. Label the five legs and the two plateau temperatures. Draw the shape only: the sim's curve is not to scale.

items.prompt: Boiling 1 g of water takes 2230 J, but melting it takes only 333 J. Use the molecule view to explain why.
items.answer: Melting only loosens the solid so molecules can slide past each other; most attractions remain. Boiling pulls the molecules completely apart into a gas, so it must overcome nearly all intermolecular forces: about 6.7 times more energy.

items.prompt: Which substance has the strongest intermolecular forces? Give two pieces of evidence from your table.
items.answer: Water: it has the highest boiling point (100 °C vs. 78 °C and 56 °C) and the largest ΔH_v (2230 J vs. 841 J and 518 J). Accept: water has hydrogen bonding.

items.prompt: Is each leg of the heating curve endothermic or exothermic? What would ΔH be for condensing 1 g of steam at 100 °C?
items.answer: Every leg is endothermic: heat is absorbed and every ΔH is positive. Condensing is the reverse of boiling, so ΔH = **−2230 J** (exothermic).

blocks.text: Tap **Run simulation** to watch water go from solid to vapor in one run. Then run acetone. Which leg takes the biggest share of the total heat for each substance?

blocks.title: Set up, part A
items: Open the menu: **Part 3 · Simulation 3: Bond enthalpies, formation, and Hess's law**. Click **Guided**. Choose a compound: **HCl**.
**Swipe sideways** across each molecule to break it. Then **swipe up or down** in each column to form an H—Cl bond. **Stop after the first H—Cl bond forms** and do the first Calculate box.
Bond energies are per mole of bonds: write them in **kJ/mol** (the sim writes only "kJ").
blocks.subtitle: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl

items.prompt: Does breaking a bond absorb energy or release energy? What about forming a bond?
items.answer: Breaking a bond absorbs energy (endothermic). Forming a bond releases energy (exothermic).

items: Energy is involved in the {{breaking}} of atoms' bonds.
Breaking H—H cost about {{436}} kJ per mole of bonds. Breaking Cl—Cl took {{242}} kJ.
Forming an H—Cl bond {{released}} {{431}} kJ.
Breaking bonds {{costs}} energy; forming bonds {{returns}} it.
ΔH°rxn = ΣΔH°(bonds broken) − ΣΔH°(bonds formed)

items.prompt: Calculate ΔH°rxn for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Then give ΔH for making **1 mole** of HCl.

blocks.title: Set up, part B
items: Form the second H—Cl bond. In the end-of-tour popup tap **Next** (or choose **C2H6**).
**Tap** each C(s) block, **swipe** each H₂, then **swipe** the two carbon groups together. **Stop after the C—C bond forms** and do the second Calculate box **before** you tap Next.
blocks.subtitle: 2C(s) + 3H₂ → C₂H₆

items: Energy is required to change the {{physical state}} of molecules.
About {{719}} kJ per mole went into turning the first carbon from C(s) into C(g).
Forming the C—C bond released {{347}} kJ.

items.prompt: Each C—H bond formed releases **414 kJ** (the sim shows this in the next step). Carbon starts as a solid, so add the sublimation energy: ΔH°rxn = ΣΔH°(bonds broken) − ΣΔH°(bonds formed) + ΣΔH°(sublimation). Calculate ΔH°rxn for 2C(s) + 3H₂ → C₂H₆.

blocks.subtitle: Finish the C₂H₆ tour, then fill in the table from the sim's bond tables.

items.prompt: Is the formation of HCl exothermic or endothermic? Use the energy absorbed and released as evidence.
items.answer: Exothermic. Breaking bonds absorbs 436 + 242 = 678 kJ; forming two H—Cl bonds releases 862 kJ. More energy is released than absorbed, so ΔH°rxn = −184 kJ (−92 kJ per mole of HCl).

items.prompt: Why does the C₂H₆ reaction need a sublimation term but the HCl reaction does not?
items.answer: Bond enthalpies are for atoms in the gas phase. Carbon starts as a solid, so 719 kJ per mole of C must first turn C(s) into C(g). H₂ and Cl₂ are already gases.

blocks.text: Look at the enthalpy diagram after the last C—H bond. Match every up arrow and down arrow to a row of your table. Which total is larger: up or down?

items: Open the menu: **Part 4: Formation Enthalpies**. Click **Guided**. Reaction type: **Exothermic** (the sim starts here). Reaction: C₂H₆ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + HCl.
The ΔH°f table is on screen from the start (values in **kJ/mol**; the sim leaves off the unit). Copy it and do the Calculate box **before** you add the reactants.

Then tap each dispenser twice (move, then pour), use the **flame slider** to reach the activation energy, and tap **Next** to run. Then tap **Next: Endothermic** and repeat. The endothermic values are **hypothetical**: made up to show what an endothermic reaction looks like.

items.prompt: If you turn the flame up higher, will ΔH°rxn change? Predict before you run.
items.answer: No. The flame only supplies the energy to get over the activation energy; ΔH°rxn depends only on the ΔH°f values of products and reactants. Accept any prediction with a reason.

blocks.subtitle: ΔH°f values in kJ/mol, copied from the sim's table for each reaction type. Compare C₂H₆ and HCl with your Part 3 results.

items: ΔH°rxn = ΣΔH°f(products) − ΣΔH°f(reactants)

items.prompt: Calculate ΔH°rxn for the **Exothermic** data set.
Calculate ΔH°rxn for the **Endothermic (hypothetical)** data set.

items: With sufficient {{energy}}, reactants will turn into products!
Use the flame slider to reach the {{Activation Energy}} and make the reaction happen.
The burner never moves the reactant or product {{plateaus}}; those come only from the tabulated {{ΔH°f}} values.
Cl₂ is listed with ΔH°f = {{0}}, because it is an {{element}} in its standard state.
blocks.subtitle: Fill in the blanks while you run the simulation

blocks.answer: Reactant plateau, a hump up to the transition state, then down to a product plateau **below** the reactants. Eₐ = arrow from reactants up to the peak. ΔH°rxn = downward arrow from reactants to products. (Endothermic: products end **above** reactants.)
blocks.subtitle: Sketch the energy diagram for the exothermic run: reactants, transition state, products. Label Eₐ and ΔH°rxn. Shape only: the sim gives no number for Eₐ and its diagram is not to scale.

items.prompt: In Part 3 you found ΔH°f of HCl = −92 kJ/mol. Use this to explain why the endothermic data set must be hypothetical.
items.answer: A substance has only one ΔH°f. The endothermic set gives HCl +20 (and C₂H₅Cl +15), which contradicts −92 from Part 3 and the exothermic set. The values were made up to show an endothermic diagram.

conclusion.prompt: Name one endothermic process and one exothermic process from this unit. Give a number from the sim for each.
conclusion.answer: Endothermic examples: water absorbing 1652 J from iron (Part 1); boiling 1 g of water, +2230 J (Part 2); breaking H—H, 436 kJ (Part 3). Exothermic examples: iron losing 1652 J (Part 1); forming H—Cl, −431 kJ (Part 3); C₂H₆ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + HCl, −120 kJ/mol (Part 4). Any correct pair with numbers.

conclusion.prompt: Part 3 (bond enthalpies) and Part 4 (ΔH°f table) both give the enthalpy of forming 1 mole of HCl. Compare the two values and explain why two different methods can give the same ΔH.
conclusion.answer: Both give −92 kJ/mol. Enthalpy is a state function: ΔH depends only on the starting and ending substances, not on the path taken. This is the idea behind Hess's law.

conclusion.prompt: Melting 1 g of ice takes 333 J; breaking 1 mole of H—H bonds takes 436 kJ. Convert water's ΔH_f to kJ/mol (H₂O = 18.0 g/mol) and compare. Which are stronger: intermolecular forces or covalent bonds?
conclusion.answer: 333 J/g × 18.0 g/mol = 5994 J/mol ≈ **6.0 kJ/mol**, far smaller than 436 kJ/mol. Covalent bonds are much stronger than intermolecular forces.

key_notes: Sim values vs. textbooks: water c = 4.2 J/g·°C (textbooks 4.184); ice 2.1 and steam 1.9 (textbooks about 2.09 and 2.01); water ΔH_vap = 2230 J/g (textbooks about 2260); C(s) → C(g) = 719 kJ/mol (textbooks about 717). The worksheet uses the sim's numbers so answers match the screen. Tell students textbooks round these a little differently.

Part 1: the burner starts on the lowest setting (40 °C) when the sim first opens and resets to lowest whenever the metal changes, including the Next → aluminum and Next → lithium steps. Guided-mode Reset and switching back to Guided set it to the highest (100 °C). The worksheet names the setting; check that the formula line shows "− 100".
Part 1: the bottom formula line shows "− 1652 J = 1652 J". The minus sign is the one in −q_system, and the box holds +1652. Students should read q from the right-hand box.
Part 1: a student who uses the rounded T_f (26.6 °C) gets q = 1663 J; the sim shows 1652 J because it uses T_f = 26.56 °C. Accept 1650–1665 J (similar for Al: 3046–3049 J; Li: 8366–8377 J).
Part 1: masses show only in the formula line (the slider readouts are hidden). The mass buttons move 5 g at a time; the water slider moves 1 g at a time, so leaving it at the 60 g default is easiest.
Part 2: every value is for 1 g and the sim never says so. The equations box labels the heat capacity "Cw" for every substance and phase; the worksheet uses Cₚ. Energies are in J (for 1 g).

Part 2: while the substance is still solid, the speech bubble says liquid Cₚ will be 4.2 J/g·°C for every substance. That is only true for water (ethanol 2.44, acetone 2.18). The correct value appears once the substance melts.

Parts 2, 3 and 4: none of the graphs are to scale (equal-size heating-curve legs; schematic bond-energy arrows; Part 4 diagram with no Eₐ number and different plateau gaps for −120 and +120). The worksheet asks only for shapes.

Part 3: the ΔH° result appears on screen the moment the last bond of each type forms (−184 when the second H—Cl forms; −85 as soon as Next is tapped after C—C). The worksheet puts each Calculate box before that point and gives C—H = 414 kJ in the prompt, because the sim shows it only in the step that also reveals −85.

Part 4: the sim calls the exothermic set "hypothetical" and does not label the endothermic set. In fact the exothermic values (C₂H₅Cl −113, HCl −92) are close to real data, and the endothermic values (+15, +20) are invented and contradict Part 3. The worksheet labels the endothermic set hypothetical.
The sim uses both ΔH°rx and ΔH°rxn; the worksheet uses ΔH°rxn throughout. The sim writes reaction enthalpies as "kJ"; the worksheet uses kJ/mol for bond energies and ΔH°f values.

Hess's law (6.9) is listed in the Part 3 and Part 4 menus but the sim has no Hess's law activity. Conclusion question 2 introduces the state-function idea; teach Hess's law with your usual lesson (Day 4).

lesson_plan.sim_location: ChemSims.app → Simulations → Thermodynamics Lab (Parts 1–4; Parts 91–94 are Unit 9)
lesson_plan.essential_question: Where does the energy go when things heat up, change phase, or react, and how can we calculate how much?
objectives: Use −q_system = q_surroundings and q = mcΔT to find a final temperature and the heat transferred in a calorimeter.
Explain why temperature stays constant during a phase change and calculate the total heat on a heating curve.
Estimate ΔH°rxn from bond enthalpies (bonds broken − bonds formed), including a sublimation term for solid carbon.
Calculate ΔH°rxn from enthalpies of formation and connect the sign of ΔH to an energy diagram.
prep: Run Parts 1–4 once in Guided mode. In Part 1, notice the burner starts on the lowest setting (40 °C) and resets whenever the metal changes.
Practice the Part 3 gestures: sideways swipes break molecules, up/down swipes in the HCl columns form bonds, taps sublime carbon.
The sim doesn't cover 6.9 Hess's Law (the menu lists it, but there is no Hess's law activity). Use your usual Hess's law lesson for it; Day 4 has 20 minutes set aside.
Decide whether students will self-grade or you will grade on Day 5.
prior_knowledge: Temperature vs. heat; units J and kJ
Intermolecular forces and phases of matter (Unit 3)

days.title: Teacher demo: heat transfer and calorimetry
days.goal: Students see that heat flows from hot to cold until thermal equilibrium, and use −q_system = q_surroundings to predict T_f.
days.worksheet_pages: Cover + pp. 1–3 (Heat Transfer & Calorimetry): set-up, prediction, notes, both Calculate boxes, iron row, graph
agenda: Warm-up: "A hot metal spoon goes into cold water. What happens to each temperature?"
Projected demo of Part 1 with iron (script below). Students fill Section 1 as you go.
Pairs: second Calculate box (q of water) and the graph sketch.
Quick check: "Which lost heat, the iron or the water? What is the sign of q for the iron?"

demo_script.do: Open the Thermodynamics Lab. Open the menu and choose Part 1 · Simulation 1: Heat transfer and calorimetry. Click Guided (top right).
demo_script.say: Read the bubble aloud: "Energy cannot be destroyed or created. Energy is transferred." Ask: where could energy go in a cup of water?
demo_script.students: First Guided Notes line: destroyed, created, transferred.

demo_script.do: Leave Choose a Metal on Iron. Tap Next.
demo_script.say: The bubble gives iron's specific heat, 0.45 J/g·°C. Point to the formula line: water's value is the 4.2. Ask: which needs more energy to warm by 1 °C, 1 g of iron or 1 g of water? (Water.)
demo_script.students: Specific heat blanks for iron and water.

demo_script.do: Step 1 (sample mass). Point out the ◀ ▶ buttons under the burner beaker (the bubble says "slider", but they are buttons, 5 g per click). Leave it at 50 g. Tap Next.
demo_script.say: Where can we see the mass? Only in the formula line: the −50.
demo_script.students: Set Up check: −50 in the formula line.

demo_script.do: Step 2 (burner). Drag the Burner fire slider all the way right (3 flames). Show that the formula line changes from − 40 to − 100. Tap Next.
demo_script.say: The burner has three settings: 40, 70 and 100 °C. We use 100 °C. Warn: it drops back to 40 °C every time you change the metal.
demo_script.students: Circle the burner instruction in the Set Up box.

demo_script.do: Step 3 (water). Leave the vertical slider at 60 g; point to "60 × 4.2" and "− 20" in the formula line. Tap Next.
demo_script.say: The metal is the system; the water is the surroundings. The water starts at 20 °C.

demo_script.do: Stop before dragging the tweezers. Give 2 minutes for the Predict box, then take a hand vote: closer to 20 °C or to 100 °C?
demo_script.say: Expected: closer to 20 °C, because water has the larger specific heat and more mass. Ask for a reason with every vote.

demo_script.do: Walk through the first Calculate box on the board: T_f = (50 × 0.45 × 100 + 60 × 4.2 × 20) ÷ (50 × 0.45 + 60 × 4.2).
demo_script.say: Expected answer 7290 ÷ 274.5 = 26.6 °C. Now let's test it.

demo_script.do: Drag the tweezers onto the iron until it highlights, carry it to the calorimeter, and drop it in. The graph starts by itself.
demo_script.say: Watch both curves. Which way does heat flow? (Hot iron to cold water.) When does it stop? (When both are at the same temperature: thermal equilibrium.)
demo_script.students: Notes: loses, gains, hot, cold. Graph sketch.

demo_script.do: Point to the formula boxes: T_f = 26.6 and the bottom line "− 1652 J = 1652 J".
demo_script.say: The minus sign belongs to −q_system: the iron lost 1652 J and the water gained 1652 J. Read q from the right-hand box.

demo_script.do: Stop here. Do not tap Next to aluminum.
demo_script.say: Tomorrow you'll run aluminum and lithium yourselves. When you tap Next, set the burner back to 3 flames first!
demo_script.students: Nothing new; finish the second Calculate box in pairs.

days.title: Student sim work: calorimetry and heating curves
days.goal: Students finish Part 1 with aluminum and lithium, then use Part 2 to measure the heat for each leg of a heating curve.
days.worksheet_pages: Finish pp. 1–3 (aluminum, lithium, Analyze, Explore); pp. 4–6 (Heating Curves & Phase Changes)
agenda: Recap: what does T_f depend on? Remind: reset the burner to 3 flames for each metal.
Part 1: aluminum and lithium rows, analysis questions, Explore.
Part 2: water first (stop at 100 °C for the Calculate box), then ethanol and acetone.
Checkpoint and clean-up.
circulate: Formula line reads "− 100" for every metal (burner on 3 flames). If a student has T_f = 23.0 °C for aluminum, the burner was left on 40 °C.
q values come from the right-hand box, not "−1652".
Part 2 calculations use 1 g and the sim's values (4.2, 2230, not 4.184 or 2260).
Students stopped at 100 °C and did the Calculate box before sliding to the end.
Liquid Cₚ for ethanol and acetone read after melting (2.44 and 2.18, not 4.2).
days.checkpoint: Lithium T_f = 53.2 °C, and the total for 1 g of water from −10 °C to 120 °C = 3042 J.
days.early_finishers: Part 1 Explore (burner on 40 °C, or 100 g iron) and Part 2 Explore (Run simulation with acetone).

days.title: Student sim work: bond enthalpies
days.goal: Students estimate ΔH°rxn from bond enthalpies for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl and 2C(s) + 3H₂ → C₂H₆.
agenda: Warm-up: "Does breaking a bond release energy?" (Predict box.)
HCl tour: break, stop after the first H—Cl, calculate, then finish.
C₂H₆ tour: sublime, break, form C—C, stop and calculate, then finish. Fill the bond table.
Enthalpy diagram sketch and analysis questions.
Checkpoint.
circulate: Students stop and calculate before forming the second H—Cl bond (the sim shows −184 right after).
Students stop after C—C and calculate before tapping Next (the sim shows −85 right after).
Signs: bonds broken are added, bonds formed are subtracted; sublimation is added.
2 × 431 (two H—Cl bonds) and 6 × 414 (six C—H bonds), not 1 of each.
days.checkpoint: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl: ΔH°rxn = −184 kJ (−92 kJ/mol HCl); 2C(s) + 3H₂ → C₂H₆: −85 kJ.
days.early_finishers: Section 3 Explore: match each arrow on the C₂H₆ diagram to the bond table.

days.title: Student sim work: enthalpy of formation, then Hess's law
days.goal: Students calculate ΔH°rxn from ΔH°f values and relate its sign to the energy diagram; teacher introduces Hess's law (not in the sim).
agenda: Warm-up: "In Part 3 you got −92 kJ/mol for HCl. Where might you see that number again?"
Part 4: copy the table and calculate before running; exothermic run, then endothermic (hypothetical) run; questions.
Teacher mini-lesson: Hess's law with your usual examples. Link it to Conclusion question 2 (the same −92 from two paths).
Conclusion questions (finish for homework if needed).
circulate: Calculate boxes done before pouring the reactants.
Subtraction order: products minus reactants; −(−85) becomes +85.
Students wrote "hypothetical" for the endothermic set and can say why (HCl +20 contradicts −92).
Diagram sketches show shapes only, with Eₐ and ΔH°rxn labelled.
days.checkpoint: Exothermic set ΔH°rxn = −120 kJ/mol; endothermic (hypothetical) set = +120 kJ/mol.
days.early_finishers: Section 4 Explore, then a Hess's law practice problem from your usual set.

days.title: Grading and wrap-up
days.goal: Students check their work against the key, discuss common errors, and show what they learned.
agenda: Grading: self-grade in a second pen color with the answer key, or collect for teacher grading (see the grading section).
Discussion: the most-missed items (sign of q, the burner reset, broken − formed vs. products − reactants).
AP practice question (FRQ) in pairs.
Exit ticket.

misconceptions.misconception: Cold flows from the water into the metal.
misconceptions.sim_fix: Part 1 graph: the metal curve only falls and the water curve only rises; the bubble says heat goes from the metal (system) to the water (surroundings).

misconceptions.misconception: The same amount of heat gives the same temperature change to both objects.
misconceptions.sim_fix: Iron run: 1652 J lowers the iron by 73.4 °C but raises the water by only 6.6 °C (m × c of 22.5 vs. 252 J/°C).

misconceptions.misconception: Adding heat always raises the temperature.
misconceptions.sim_fix: Part 2: the thermometer stays at 0 °C and 100 °C while 333 J and 2230 J are added; the bubble says ΔH = Cₚ × (T₂ − T₁) is zero there.
Part 3: breaking H—H costs 436 kJ; only forming H—Cl releases energy (431 kJ). The arrows go up for breaking and down for forming.

misconceptions.misconception: More heat from the burner makes the reaction release more energy.
misconceptions.sim_fix: Part 4: the plateaus never move with the flame; ΔH°rxn stays −120 kJ/mol. The flame only helps reach the activation energy.

sim_cautions: Part 1: the burner starts on the lowest setting (40 °C) and goes back to it every time the metal changes, even when you tap Next to go to aluminum. Have students check that the formula line shows "− 100".
Part 1: the bottom line reads "− 1652 J = 1652 J". The minus sign is part of −q_system; the number in the box is positive. Read q from the right-hand box.
Part 1: the bubble says "Pinch the slider" for the sample mass, but the control is a pair of ◀ ▶ buttons. It also says "press play", but the graph starts on its own after the drop.

exit_ticket.question: 60 g of water (c = 4.2 J/g·°C) warms from 20.0 °C to 32.1 °C. How much heat did it gain?
Why does the temperature stay at 100 °C while water boils, even though heat is still being added?
exit_ticket.answer: The energy goes into overcoming intermolecular forces to turn liquid into gas, not into raising the temperature.

exit_ticket.question: Using ΔH°f values C₂H₆ −85, Cl₂ 0, C₂H₅Cl −113, HCl −92 kJ/mol, find ΔH°rxn for C₂H₆ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + HCl. Exothermic or endothermic?

ap_practice.question: FRQ. A 50.0 g sample of aluminum (c = 0.897 J/g·°C) is heated to 100.0 °C and placed in 60.0 g of water (c = 4.2 J/g·°C) at 20.0 °C in an insulated calorimeter. The final temperature is 32.1 °C. (a) Calculate the heat gained by the water. (b) Calculate q for the aluminum and state whether the process is exothermic or endothermic for the aluminum. (c) Explain, in terms of particle motion, why heat stops flowing at 32.1 °C. (d) If the calorimeter were not insulated and lost heat to the room, would the specific heat of aluminum calculated from these data be too high or too low? Justify.
ap_practice.answer: (a) q_water = 60.0 × 4.2 × (32.1 − 20.0) = 3049 J ≈ 3.05 kJ. (b) q_Al = 50.0 × 0.897 × (32.1 − 100.0) = −3045 J; exothermic for the aluminum (it loses heat). (c) At 32.1 °C the metal and water particles have the same average kinetic energy, so there is no net transfer of energy: thermal equilibrium. (d) Too low: heat lost to the room makes T_f lower, so q_water is smaller and ΔT of the aluminum is larger; c = q ÷ (m × ΔT) comes out smaller.

ap_practice.question: MCQ. Bond enthalpies (kJ/mol): H—H 436, Cl—Cl 242, H—Cl 431. What is ΔH° for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g)? (A) +247 kJ (B) −184 kJ (C) −92 kJ (D) +184 kJ
ap_practice.answer: (B) −184 kJ: (436 + 242) − 2(431) = 678 − 862. (A) forgets the 2; (C) is per mole of HCl, not for the equation as written; (D) has bonds formed minus bonds broken.
